A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same logit-lens interpretation and PROJECTAWAY editing work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original COCO hallucination detection and removal experiments, parameter ablations, and ImageNet segmentation results, with additional quantitative and qualitative evidence in the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results for newer models, VQA attribute correction, COCO patch classification, and LLaVA-Bench examples.

M1.justification: The internal-confidence computation, PROJECTAWAY algorithm, and segmentation procedure remain unchanged. The appendix applies existing confidence scoring and editing to additional models and targets without introducing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained COCO and ImageNet evaluations, v2 adds VQA 2.0 color/count correction cases, caption-editing examples from LLaVA-Bench, and zero-shot multiclass classification of COCO image patches. These substantially broaden the evaluated task requirements, although the VQA and LLaVA-Bench evidence is qualitative.

E2.justification: The retained comparisons preserve their output-probability, greedy/nucleus/beam-search, OPERA, raw-attention, and TextSpan baselines. New Tables 6–7 reuse the confidence baseline and beam search. LLaVA-NeXT and Cambrian-1 are additional backbones receiving the proposed intervention, rather than new competing methods.

E3.justification: Existing protocols remain intact, but v2 adds substantial evaluation design: LLaVA-NeXT 7B and Cambrian-1 8B experiments with model-specific thresholds and 500-image evaluations, filtered low-confidence VQA cases, and segmentation-derived patch labels evaluated with top-3/5/10 accuracy. Table 8 reports 55,988 patches; these are additional protocols, not revisions to the original experiments.

E4.justification: The original layer and editing-weight ablations are unchanged. New supplementary analyses examine class-dependent patch recognition and illustrate whether editing extends to color/count errors and non-COCO images (Appendices A.7–A.9). These provide useful diagnostics and case studies, but limited systematic robustness evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new tables retain point-estimate reporting; internal object-confidence scores are prediction scores, not statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–5 and plotted results are retained. New Tables 6–7 report detection and intervention outcomes on two newer models: CHAIRs falls from 23.8 to 17.2 for LLaVA-NeXT and 9.2 to 6.6 for Cambrian-1, with recall unchanged against each model's beam-search baseline. Table 8 adds overall top-3/5/10 accuracies of 32.7/39.3/52.2%, alongside new qualitative outcomes. These are new experiments, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, confidence formula, and projection-based editing reasoning are unchanged. No theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims about interpreting image representations, reducing hallucinations without training, and enabling segmentation. Additional appendix evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix A.8 newly hypothesizes that class-dependent recognition reflects alternative lexical representations, such as 'doctor' or 'skier' instead of 'person'. Appendices A.7 and A.9 explain the focus on objects and COCO through sparse attribute-evaluation tooling and CHAIR's dataset dependence, while interpreting the added examples as evidence of broader applicability.

D1.justification: v2 specifies thresholds of 0.4 and 0.3 for the newer models and editing parameters (24, 22, 2), including their selection rationale. It also documents the 0.05 attribute threshold and reuse of InstructBLIP parameters for the new examples. Existing implementation disclosures and code-access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for LLaVA-NeXT and Cambrian-1 and removes Shaham et al. (2024), 'A multimodal automated interpretability agent'. The broader related-work discussion and positioning of the contribution remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is preserved. v2 adds four appendix subsections, moves object localization from A.5 to A.6, corrects hallucination-detection cross-references to Table 5, and makes small wording and conference-header edits. There is no extensive rewriting of the main narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 6–8 and two qualitative figures for attributes and LLaVA-Bench. Existing appendix tables and ablation plots are repositioned, and old Figures 12–16 become Figures 14–18. The original main figures, table structures, and graphical content are preserved.

improvement.justification: The newer-model comparisons strengthen evidence of transfer, while the classwise analysis exposes a useful applicability boundary absent from v1. The gains are bounded because attribute and non-COCO extensions remain illustrative. A small reporting inconsistency also appears: Appendix A.5 claims a 28.86% Cambrian-1 CHAIRs reduction, whereas Table 7's 9.2-to-6.6 change implies about 28.26%. Overall, the added evidence provides a limited but clear quality improvement.
